cheatsheet:
**A connected pair** (`<sys/socket.h>`)
`int fds[2]; socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0, fds);`

**Bytes in, bytes out**
`send(fd, data, n, 0)` · `ssize_t got = recv(fd, buf, room, 0)`: 0 = other side hung up, -1 = error · add the `'\0'` yourself

**Two processes** (`<unistd.h>`, `<sys/wait.h>`)
`pid_t pid = fork();` 0 in the child · each side `close`s the end it doesn't use · child ends with `_exit(0)` · parent `waitpid(pid, NULL, 0)`

**Protocols**
Send an int's bytes: `send(fd, &v, sizeof v, 0)` · read whole ones with `MSG_WAITALL` · `shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR)` = done sending

**On a real network**
`socket`, then `bind`/`listen`/`accept` on the server and `connect` on the client; send/recv work the same.

lessons.title: A socket is a phone line
lessons.concept:
A **socket** is one end of a connection between two programs. What you `send` into one end comes out of the other with `recv`. Over the internet the ends are on different machines; here they're in the same program.

`socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0, fds)` makes two connected ends, `fds[0]` and `fds[1]`. Each is just a number, like a FILE but lower level.

`send(fd, data, how_many_bytes, 0)` and `recv(fd, buffer, room, 0)` move raw **bytes**: recv returns how many arrived, and it doesn't add a `'\0'` for you.

predict.prompt: Before you run it: type what it prints.
predict.explain: Six bytes go in at fds[0] and come out at fds[1]. The program adds the '\0' itself before printing.

drills.code: ssize_t got = recv(fd, buf, sizeof buf, 0);
options: How many bytes arrived (0 means the other side hung up, -1 an error)
drills.answer: How many bytes arrived (0 means the other side hung up, -1 an error)
drills.explain: That count is how you know where the message ends, and where to put the '\0'.

drills.prompt: Send the word through the socket and report how many bytes arrived. The count comes out wrong for most words. Fix it.
drills.explain: `msg` is a pointer, so `sizeof msg` is the size of an address (8 bytes), not the length of the text. `strlen(msg)` counts the characters.
The line works both ways: ping goes 0 → 1, pong goes 1 → 0. (The arrays start zeroed, so the strings are already terminated.)

drills.prompt: One end sends `"AB"`, then `"CD"`. The other end does one `recv` with room for 10 bytes. What can it get?
options: Possibly ABCD all at once: a stream has no message boundaries
An error: it must ask for exactly 2
drills.answer: Possibly ABCD all at once: a stream has no message boundaries
drills.explain: SOCK_STREAM is a stream of bytes, not separate messages. If you need boundaries, build them in (lesson 3).

drills.prompt: Read a word. Send it from `fds[0]`, receive it at `fds[1]`, turn it UPPERCASE, send it back from `fds[1]`, receive it at `fds[0]`, and print `reply: WORD`.
drills.explain: Use recv's count everywhere: for the uppercase loop, for how much to send back, and for where the '\0' goes.

lessons.title: Two programs: fork
lessons.concept:
`fork()` copies the running program. Both copies carry on from the same line; fork returns **0 in the child** and the child's id in the parent. That's how each knows its role.

Make the socketpair **before** forking and both get both ends. Each side keeps one: the child closes `fds[0]` and talks on `fds[1]`, the parent the other way round. Now it's a real conversation between two programs.

The parent waits for the child with `waitpid(pid, NULL, 0)`. The child ends with `_exit(0)`, which leaves without flushing the copy of printf's buffer it inherited.

predict.prompt: Before you run it: type what it prints.
predict.explain: The parent sends `help us`; the child uppercases it and sends it back. Only the parent prints.

drills.prompt: What does `fork()` return in the child?
drills.explain: The parent gets the child's id (and -1 if fork failed); the child gets 0.

drills.prompt: Type what this prints (when the output goes to a file, as on the judge).
drills.explain: `ping` was still sitting in printf's buffer when fork copied the program, buffer and all. Both copies flush it when they finish. `fflush(stdout)` before fork, or `_exit(0)` in the child, prevents it.

drills.prompt: Order and indent the lines into a parent and child that each close the end they don't use **first**, then do their job.
drills.explain: The child's branch ends in `_exit`, so everything after the `}` only runs in the parent.

drills.prompt: The beacon should send the message back in UPPERCASE, but the parent gets an empty reply. Fix the child.
drills.explain: The child closed `fds[1]`, the very end it talks on, so its recv and send fail and the station never gets an answer. Each side closes the **other** end: the one it doesn't use.

lessons.title: Request, reply, hang up
lessons.concept:
Two programs need to agree on what the bytes mean: a **protocol**. The simplest is to send an int's own bytes: `send(fd, &v, sizeof v, 0)`, and on the other side `recv` into an int.

recv may hand you fewer bytes than you asked for. `MSG_WAITALL` makes it wait until it has them all (or the line closes), so a 4-byte read gives you a whole int.

How does the server know the client is finished? The client calls `shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR)`: *I'm done sending, but still listening*. The server's next recv returns 0, and it sends its answer.

predict.prompt: Before you run it: type what it prints.
predict.explain: The server adds 12, 30 and 7 until shutdown makes its recv return 0, then sends back 49.

drills.prompt: What does `shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR)` tell the other side?
options: I'm done sending: your recv will return 0, but I can still receive your reply
Close the whole connection right now
drills.answer: I'm done sending: your recv will return 0, but I can still receive your reply
drills.explain: That half-close is what lets the server finish its loop and still answer.

drills.prompt: Why does the server use `MSG_WAITALL` when it reads an int?
options: recv may return just part of the int; MSG_WAITALL waits for all 4 bytes (or the end)
Without it recv returns a string
It makes recv skip bad data
drills.answer: recv may return just part of the int; MSG_WAITALL waits for all 4 bytes (or the end)
drills.explain: On a stream, half an int can arrive. Waiting for the full size keeps the two sides in step.

drills.prompt: The station sends `n` ints (n ≥ 1), then shuts down its sending side, then expects **two** ints back: how many it sent and the biggest. Write the beacon's `serve`. The rest is done.
drills.explain: Loop until recv stops returning a whole int, track the count and the max (starting from the first value, since they may all be negative), then send both in one go.

checkpoint.prompt: What does `socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0, fds)` give you?
options: Two connected ends: what goes into one comes out of the other
checkpoint.answer: Two connected ends: what goes into one comes out of the other
checkpoint.explain: Both ends work in both directions.

checkpoint.prompt: After fork, how do the two copies tell which one they are?
options: fork returns 0 in the child and the child's id in the parent
The child gets a different main
checkpoint.answer: fork returns 0 in the child and the child's id in the parent

checkpoint.explain: The array's 12 bytes (3 ints of 4) arrive as they were sent: 4 + 5 + 6 = 15.

checkpoint.prompt: recv returned 0. What does that mean?
checkpoint.code: ssize_t n = recv(fd, buf, sizeof buf, 0);
options: The other side closed or shut down sending: no more data is coming
checkpoint.answer: The other side closed or shut down sending: no more data is coming
checkpoint.explain: 0 is the end-of-conversation signal, like EOF for files.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does the child finish with `_exit(0)` instead of `return 0`?
options: It leaves without flushing the stdout buffer it copied from the parent, so nothing prints twice
return doesn't work in a child
checkpoint.answer: It leaves without flushing the stdout buffer it copied from the parent, so nothing prints twice
checkpoint.explain: Remember `ping ping`: the child inherited the parent's unprinted output.
